name: Law of Demeter and Tell, Don't Ask
intent: Let each piece of code talk to the objects it holds directly, and tell them what to do instead of reaching through them for data to decide with, so a change inside one class stays inside it.
scenario: An online shop computes tax in a dozen places, each by walking from the order to the customer, the customer's address, the address's country and the country's rate. Then customers get a separate shipping address, and the old address field becomes the billing one. Every one of those call sites still runs, and every one now charges tax by the billing country.
problem: The Law of Demeter says a method should only call methods on itself, on its parameters, on objects it creates, and on its own direct parts: talk to friends, not to friends of friends. It is often reduced to 'no more than one dot', and that reading goes wrong both ways. A call like order.customer.address.country.rate spreads knowledge of four classes into every caller, so a change in a distant class breaks code that never mentioned it. But the cure applied mechanically, a forwarding method for every piece of data in every class, trades long chains for a thicket of boilerplate and does not move any decision to where the data lives.

howItWorks.title: See what a chain really says
howItWorks.text: In order.customer.address.country.rate, the caller knows that an order has a customer, that a customer has an address, that an address has a country, and that a country has a rate. Each of those is a fact about someone else's internals. Change any of them, for instance a customer now has two addresses, and every caller that walked through that link is affected, even if it only wanted the tax. In the sample, the old code keeps running after that change and quietly uses the billing country: 190 where 200 is right.

howItWorks.title: Tell, do not ask
howItWorks.text: Tell, Don't Ask is the companion rule. Instead of fetching data from an object and deciding outside it, tell the object to do the job: order.tax(). The order knows its customer, the customer knows which address tax follows, and the rule lives in one place. When the rule changes, one method changes, and the callers, which never knew the structure, are untouched. The sample fixes the shipping-address change in one method, in one class.

howItWorks.title: Count where the edits land
howItWorks.text: The simulation counts the edits for four changes in a model with 12 call sites. With train-wreck calls, restructuring how a customer holds its address means editing 9 call sites in 7 modules. With tell, it is 4 one-line edits in one class. The number of edits matters less than where they are: one class with its own tests, against seven modules that each need re-checking.

howItWorks.title: Know what the rule does not cover
howItWorks.text: Demeter is about objects with behaviour and hidden structure. Walking a plain data structure, such as a parsed JSON document or a record returned by a query, exposes no internals that were meant to be hidden. A fluent builder or a stream pipeline returns the same type each time, so a long line of dots there is one conversation with one object. Counting dots is a poor test: ask whether the caller has to know how someone else is built.

howItWorks.title: Stop before the wrapper explosion
howItWorks.text: The over-applied extreme is to give every class a forwarding method for every piece of data behind it: order.customerAddressCountryRate(), customer.addressCountryRate(), and so on. Chains disappear, but the order now exposes 8 methods and the classes together hold 18 that only forward. Adding one field at the far end means adding a hop in every class on the way down: 5 edits instead of 1. And because callers still ask for the rate and decide, the tax rule is still copied at each caller. Forwarding hides the path but does not tell anyone to do anything.

pros: A change in a distant class stays local, so fewer modules need editing and re-testing
Behaviour sits next to the data it uses, so each rule has one home
Callers read as intent (order.tax()) instead of as navigation
Classes can restructure their internals without breaking the code that uses them
cons: Classes grow more methods, and a class that answers every question for its parts can become a catch-all
Each hop of delegation is another method to write, name and test
It is hard to apply to reporting and display code, which truly needs to read many values
Teams can follow the letter (no long chains) while keeping the problem (callers still decide everything)
whenToUse: Domain objects with real behaviour and hidden structure, such as orders, accounts and customers
Any rule that several call sites currently compute by reaching through the same chain
Code at module boundaries, where one module should not depend on how another is built
whenNotToUse: Plain data records and JSON-like structures, where navigating them is the point
Fluent interfaces and pipelines that return the same type, where the dots are one conversation
Read-only views, queries and reports, which are usually better served by a query that returns exactly the shape they need
pitfalls: Counting dots instead of asking what the caller must know: a builder chain is fine, a four-object walk is not
Adding a getter for every field of a part to the whole, so the structure is hidden in name only and the callers still decide everything
Moving a chain into a helper function that every caller calls: the knowledge is now in one place, but a utility that reaches through four classes is itself a train wreck
Forcing display and persistence logic into domain objects because 'tell, don't ask' says so, until a customer class knows how to print HTML
Applying Demeter to data transfer objects and then writing wrapper methods for plain fields
Forgetting that old code keeps compiling when a meaning changes: a train-wreck call after the 'address' field changes meaning is wrong with no error to point to it
Treating a failing chain in a test as the problem, then mocking each link: tests that must stub four objects are telling you the code asks too much

roles.label: Call site
roles.description: Code that needs an answer, such as a tax amount or a shipping label.

roles.label: Order
roles.description: The object the callers hold and talk to.

roles.label: Inner classes
roles.description: Customer, address and country: structure the callers should not need to know.

roles.label: Change request
roles.description: A new requirement that alters how something is held or computed.

quiz.question: Twelve call sites compute tax with order.customer.address.country.rate. Customers now get a second address. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The chain is slow, because each dot adds a method call.
Every call site knows how customers hold addresses, so all of them are affected by the change.
Chains cannot be tested, because each step needs its own test double.
The rate should be a constant, since a rate never depends on the customer.
quiz.explanation: The issue is knowledge, not speed. Each caller depends on the structure of four classes, so a change in one of them reaches every caller, and here the old calls keep running and silently give the wrong result.

quiz.question: A team removes every chain by adding forwarding methods to every class for every field behind it. What do they most likely end up with?
options: A design where each rule lives in exactly one place, because callers can no longer see the structure.
Fewer methods overall, since the chains are gone and callers use one method each.
Many boilerplate methods, a wider public surface, and callers that still make the decisions.
A design that breaks the Law of Demeter, because forwarding is itself a chain.
quiz.explanation: Forwarding every field hides the path but not the data flow: callers still ask and decide, so rules stay copied, and each new field needs a hop in every class above it. Telling an object to do the job is what moves the rule.

quiz.question: Which of these is the weakest case for applying the Law of Demeter?
options: A pipeline call such as list.filter(...).map(...).first(), which returns the same kind of object each step.
An order calling customer.taxOn(total) on a customer it holds directly.
A checkout method calling a method on the payment object passed to it as a parameter.
A service asking order.customer.address.country.rate to decide a discount.
quiz.explanation: A fluent pipeline is one conversation with one kind of object, and no internals are exposed, so counting its dots misses the point. The service reaching through order, customer, address and country is the classic train wreck, and the other calls stay within direct parts and parameters.
